Scalars and Vectors.intro: Physical quantities can be either scalar (magnitude only) or vector (magnitude and direction). This distinction is fundamental to understanding forces.

sections.title: Scalars vs Vectors
points: Scalar — magnitude only: speed, distance, mass, energy, temperature, time
Vector — magnitude AND direction: velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, momentum
Vectors can be represented by arrows — length = magnitude, direction = direction

sections.title: Adding Vectors
points: Vectors in same direction: add magnitudes
Vectors in opposite directions: subtract magnitudes
Vectors at angles: use scale drawing or Pythagoras

keyTerms.def: A quantity with magnitude only — no direction (e.g. speed, mass)
A quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g. velocity, force)
The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors combined

examTips: Speed is scalar; velocity is vector. Distance is scalar; displacement is vector.
When forces are balanced (resultant = 0), the object is in equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Saying speed and velocity are the same — velocity has direction, speed does not.
Forgetting direction when describing a vector quantity.

Forces.intro: Forces are pushes or pulls that can change the speed, direction or shape of an object. Understanding forces and their effects is central to P5.

sections.title: Contact and Non-Contact Forces
points: Contact forces: friction, normal force, tension, air resistance
Non-contact forces: gravity (weight), magnetic force, electrostatic force

sections.title: Resultant Force
points: Multiple forces can be replaced by a single resultant force
Balanced forces (resultant = 0): object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity
Unbalanced forces (resultant ≠ 0): object accelerates in direction of resultant

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: W = m × g (Weight = mass × gravitational field strength). On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg. Weight is a FORCE (newtons); mass is an amount of matter (kilograms).

keyTerms.def: A push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape — measured in newtons
The gravitational force on an object: W = mg
The single force that represents the combined effect of all forces on an object
State where all forces are balanced — no acceleration

examTips: Weight = mg. On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg ≈ 10 N/kg.
Balanced forces ≠ no forces. Balanced forces mean NO ACCELERATION.
Friction always acts opposite to direction of motion.
commonMistakes: Confusing mass (kg) and weight (N) — they are different quantities.
Saying balanced forces mean the object is stationary — it could be moving at constant velocity.

Work Done.intro: Work is done when a force causes an object to move. It is a measure of energy transferred.

sections.title: Work Done Formula

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: W = F × d (Work done = Force × distance moved in direction of force). Units: joules (J). 1 J = 1 N × 1 m.

points: Work done = energy transferred
If force and displacement are in same direction: W = Fd
No work done if force is perpendicular to displacement (e.g. gravity on horizontal motion)

callout.label: Power Formula
callout.text: P = W/t (Power = Work done ÷ time). Units: watts (W). Also P = Fv (Power = Force × velocity).

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object: W = Fd (joules)
Rate of doing work: P = W/t (watts)
Unit of energy and work — 1 J = 1 N × 1 m

examTips: Work done = energy transferred — they are equivalent.
P = W/t and P = Fv are both useful — choose depending on what's given.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that work requires movement — a force without movement does no work.
Using distance instead of displacement in direction of force.

Elasticity.intro: Elastic materials return to their original shape after a force is removed. Hooke's Law describes the relationship between force and extension.

sections.title: Hooke's Law

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: F = k × e (Force = spring constant × extension). Spring constant k is in N/m. Hooke's Law applies up to the LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY.

points: Extension proportional to force — graph is a straight line through origin
Beyond limit of proportionality: permanent deformation; spring doesn't return to original length

sections.title: Elastic and Inelastic
points: Elastic deformation — returns to original shape when force removed
Inelastic (plastic) deformation — does not return to original shape — permanently changed
Elastic potential energy stored: Ee = ½ke²

keyTerms.def: Extension is proportional to force: F = ke — valid up to limit of proportionality
Measure of stiffness of a spring: k = F/e (N/m)
Deformation that is reversed when force is removed
Point beyond which Hooke's Law no longer applies

examTips: F = ke — steeper gradient on F-e graph = larger spring constant = stiffer spring.
Elastic potential energy: Ee = ½ke².
commonMistakes: Saying elastic means stretchy — elastic means it returns to original shape.
Forgetting that Hooke's Law only applies up to the limit of proportionality.

Motion.intro: Motion can be described using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Distance-time and velocity-time graphs are essential tools.

sections.title: Key Definitions
points: Speed — distance ÷ time (m/s) — scalar
Velocity — displacement ÷ time (m/s) — vector
Acceleration — change in velocity ÷ time (m/s²) — vector

sections.title: Distance-Time Graphs
points: Gradient = speed
Flat line = stationary
Straight line = constant speed
Curved line = changing speed (acceleration/deceleration)

sections.title: Velocity-Time Graphs
points: Gradient = acceleration
Area under graph = distance travelled
Flat line = constant velocity
Positive gradient = acceleration; Negative gradient = deceleration

callout.label: Key Equations
callout.text: v = u + at | s = ut + ½at² | v² = u² + 2as | s = (u+v)/2 × t. (s=displacement, u=initial velocity, v=final velocity, a=acceleration, t=time)

keyTerms.def: Rate of change of velocity — change in velocity ÷ time (m/s²)
Speed in a given direction — a vector quantity
Distance in a specified direction from a reference point

examTips: v-t graph: gradient = acceleration. Area = distance.
d-t graph: gradient = speed. Flat = stationary.
Deceleration is negative acceleration — state the direction.
commonMistakes: Reading gradient of d-t graph as acceleration — it gives SPEED.
Forgetting area under v-t graph = distance (not just for triangles — also trapeziums).

Newton's Laws.intro: Newton's three laws of motion describe the relationship between force, mass and acceleration. They are fundamental to understanding how objects move.

sections.title: Newton's First Law

callout.label: First Law
callout.text: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force.

points: Balanced forces → no acceleration (stays at rest or constant velocity)
Inertia = tendency of objects to resist changes in motion

sections.title: Newton's Second Law

callout.label: Second Law
callout.text: F = ma (Resultant force = mass × acceleration). Units: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s².

points: Larger force → greater acceleration
Larger mass → smaller acceleration (for same force)
Direction of acceleration = direction of resultant force

callout.label: Third Law
callout.text: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces act on DIFFERENT objects — they cannot cancel each other out.

keyTerms.def: Objects stay at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts
Resultant force = mass × acceleration: F = ma
Equal and opposite reaction forces — act on different objects
Tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion

examTips: F = ma — rearrange for a = F/m or m = F/a.
Third law pairs: act on DIFFERENT objects; same type of force; equal magnitude; opposite direction.
Balanced forces ≠ no forces — balanced means ZERO resultant.
commonMistakes: Saying third law forces cancel — they can't, they act on different objects.
Confusing balanced forces (no acceleration) with zero forces (nothing touching).

Stopping Distances.intro: The total stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of thinking distance and braking distance. Both are affected by different factors.

sections.title: Stopping Distance

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Total stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

points: Thinking distance: distance travelled while driver reacts
Braking distance: distance travelled while brakes are applied

sections.title: Factors Affecting Each
points: Thinking distance increases with: higher speed, driver tiredness, alcohol/drugs, distraction
Braking distance increases with: higher speed, worn tyres, wet/icy road, worn brakes, heavier vehicle

sections.title: Reaction Time
points: Typical reaction time: 0.2–0.9 seconds
Measured by: ruler drop test or computer-based tests
Increased by: alcohol, drugs, tiredness, distractions

keyTerms.def: Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time
Distance travelled after brakes are applied until vehicle stops
Time between a stimulus and a response — typically 0.2-0.9 s

examTips: Speed affects BOTH thinking distance AND braking distance — very important.
Braking distance ∝ v² — doubling speed quadruples braking distance.
commonMistakes: Saying only road conditions affect stopping distance — reaction time affects thinking distance.
Forgetting that speed affects both components of stopping distance.

Momentum.intro: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity. It is conserved in all collisions and explosions (in the absence of external forces).

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: p = m × v (Momentum = mass × velocity). Units: kg m/s. Momentum is a vector quantity.

sections.title: Conservation of Momentum
points: Total momentum before = total momentum after (in a closed system)
Applies to collisions and explosions
In explosion from rest: total momentum = 0 (equal and opposite momenta)

callout.label: Force and Momentum
callout.text: F = Δp/Δt (Force = change in momentum ÷ time). Rearranged: F × t = Δp (impulse = change in momentum). Larger time → smaller force for same momentum change — explains crumple zones.

keyTerms.def: Mass × velocity — a vector quantity measured in kg m/s
Total momentum before = total momentum after in a closed system
Change in momentum = force × time (N s or kg m/s)

examTips: Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions — elastic and inelastic.
Crumple zones increase collision time → smaller force for same momentum change → less injury.
In explosion from rest: momenta are equal and opposite → total = 0.
commonMistakes: Forgetting momentum is a vector — direction matters in calculations.
Saying kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions — only in elastic collisions.
